title: Linear Equations in Two Variables, Part 1: The Idea and an Easy Problem

beats.say: A linear equation in two variables, such as y equals two x minus four, describes a straight line on the coordinate plane. Every point on that line is a solution of the equation.

card.text: A line is a set of solutions

beats.say: The SAT asks you to move between slope-intercept form and standard form, find intercepts, and write equations for parallel or perpendicular lines.
It also asks you to set up equations from stories, such as tickets at two different prices that add up to a fixed total.
A point p comma q is on a line exactly when putting x equals p and y equals q into the equation makes it true. That is how you test any point.
beats.item: On the line means it makes the equation true

beats.say: In the form y equals m x plus b, you can read the slope m and the y-intercept b directly from the equation.
beats.item: y = mx + b shows slope and intercept

beats.say: In standard form, A x plus B y equals C, the intercepts are quick. Set x to zero to find the y-intercept, and set y to zero to find the x-intercept.
beats.item: Standard form: set one variable to zero

beats.say: In a story equation like eight a plus five c equals two hundred, each coefficient is a price per item, and the constant is the total. An intercept means all of one kind.
Parallel lines have equal slopes. Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, so their product is negative one.
This table shows where to find the slope and the intercepts in each form. In slope-intercept form, the slope is m, the y-intercept is b, and the x-intercept is negative b over m.
In standard form, the slope is negative A over B, the y-intercept is C over B, and the x-intercept is C over A. The minus sign in the slope is easy to forget.
Easy example. Find the slope and both intercepts of the line six x minus three y equals twelve. We will find each one with its own short calculation.

card.sub: Find the slope and both intercepts

beats.say: For standard form, the slope is negative A over B. Here A is six and B is negative three, so we write negative six over negative three.
Six divided by negative three is negative two, and the minus sign in front flips it. So the slope is two.
To find the y-intercept, set x equal to zero. That is the point where the line crosses the y axis, so x is zero there.
Six times zero is zero, so the equation becomes negative three y equals twelve.
Divide both sides by negative three. Twelve divided by negative three is negative four. So the y-intercept is negative four.
To find the x-intercept, set y equal to zero. That is where the line crosses the x axis.
Negative three times zero is zero, so the equation becomes six x equals twelve.
Divide both sides by six. Twelve divided by six is two. So the x-intercept is two.
As a check, rewrite the equation in slope-intercept form. Start with the original equation, and get y alone.
Subtract six x from both sides, so the x term leaves the left side.
Divide every term by negative three. Negative six x divided by negative three is two x, and twelve divided by negative three is negative four.
The slope is two and the y-intercept is negative four, exactly as we found before. And when y is zero, two x minus four equals zero gives x equals two. Everything agrees.
To recap. Every point on a line makes its equation true, and slope-intercept form shows the slope and y-intercept directly.
beats.item: Points on a line satisfy the equation

beats.say: In standard form, the slope is negative A over B. For intercepts, set one variable to zero and solve for the other.
beats.item: Standard form: slope −A/B, zero a variable

beats.say: Perpendicular slopes are negative reciprocals. In the next video, we work through a medium problem and a hard problem.
